4. Experimental Results  217  
4.1. Experimental Settings  218  
The experiments were conducted using the PyTorch [29] deep learning framework  219  
in Python 3.8, within the Anaconda3 environment, and implemented using the PyCharm  220  
compiler. The training of our model consisted of 20,000 iterations, utilizing the PhraseCut+  221  
dataset. We employed a batch size of 64 and set the image size to 352×352 pixels. During  222  
the model’s training process, we employed the AdamW optimization algorithm to itera- 223  
tively optimize the network. The initial learning rate was set to 0.001. As the model ap- 224  Electronics 2024, 13, x FOR PEER REVIEW  6  of  14 
 
 
proaches the global minimum of the loss function, the corresponding learning rate grad- 225  
ually decreases towards a minimum point. To achieve this, we utilized the Cosine An- 226  
nealing method for dynamic learning rate adjustment without warm-up. The minimum  227  
learning rate was set to 0.0001. Simultaneously, we adopted the technique of automatic  228  
mixed precision to enhance the training process. Our model’s loss function exclusively  229  
employed the binary cross-entropy function.  230  
4.2. Datasets    231  
PhraseCut+ is employed as the primary dataset for our training process. It is an ex- 232  
tension of the PhraseCut dataset   [30], encompassing 345,486 phrase regions meticulously  233  
labeled with category names, attributes, and object relationships within the images. Each  234  
phrase corresponds to a binary segmentation mask in the image. PhraseCut+ enhances the  235  
original dataset by introducing visual support samples and negative samples. This aug- 236  
mentation makes it particularly well-suited for models that jointly process text and visual  237  
inputs. The dataset extends the phrase regions using automatically learned templates and  238  
ensures partial object visibility by considering object position information during random  239  
cropping.    240  
Pascal-VOC2012 [31]serves as the basis for our zero-shot image segmentation exper- 241  
iments. Pascal-VOC2012     is a comprehensive dataset featuring images for training, vali- 242  
dation, and testing. The validation subset consists of 1,449 images, each accompanied by  243  
pixel-level semantic segmentation masks used for image segmentation tasks. It includes  244  
annotations for 20 object categories along with a background category. We follow previ- 245  
ous studies’ practice [1, 28] by partitioning these 20 categories into 16 seen classes and 4  246  
unseen classes ("cow," "motorbike," "airplane," and "sofa") to evaluate open word segmen- 247  
tation performance. Additionally, we employ the Pascal-5i dataset [21], a one-shot seg- 248  
mentation dataset derived from Pascal-VOC2012, which contains 20 object classes evenly  249  
distributed across four sections.    250  
For our zero-shot segmentation experiment, we employ the Pascal-Context dataset  251  
[32], which consists of 5,105 validation samples, spanning 59 item classes in addition to a  252  
background class. Similarly to Pascal-VOC, we select four unseen categories ("cow," "mo- 253  
torbike," "sofa," and "cat") from the foreground category for evaluation.    254  
The COCO-20i dataset [33] is commonly used for one-shot segmentation tasks and  255  
is derived from the COCO dataset. It includes annotations for 80 object classes evenly  256  
divided into four sections, each containing 20 categories.    257  
The test results involve selecting the best-performing group from among these four  258  
sections. These datasets provide a diverse and comprehensive foundation for evaluating  259  
the  performance  of  our  proposed  open-vocabulary  and  multitask  image  segmentation  260  
framework.  261

Below is a **quantitative, step‑by‑step look** at how the B‑52 burns fuel in the various cruise regimes it normally uses, what that means for *unrefuelled* range, how aerial refuelling extends the picture, and – finally – how a **four‑high‑bypass‑turbofan (HB‑TF) swap** would reshape those numbers.

> **NOTE:** All figures are **rounded‑off, representative averages** taken from publicly‑available performance tables, Air Force “operating‑handbook” data, and modern turbofan SFC data (e.g., Pratt & Whitney F135, GE F110, Rolls‑Royce Eurojet EJ200). Real‑world missions will vary with payload, weather, winds, and configuration (external fuel tanks, weapons stores, etc.).

## 1. Baseline B‑52 (Eight Pratt & Whitney TF33‑P‑3/3B)

| Item | Value (typical) |
|------|-----------------|
| **Engine thrust (max)** | 17,000 lbf each → **136,000 lbf total** |
| **Specific fuel consumption (SFC) – cruise** | **0.72 lb/(lbf·h)** (TF33‑P‑3, low‑bypass turbo‑jet) |
| **Internal fuel capacity** | **315,000 lb** (≈ 47,200 US gal of JP‑8) |
| **Maximum take‑off weight (MTOW)** | 488,000 lb |
| **Typical cruise thrust setting** | 20‑25 % of max → **≈ 30‑35 k lbf total** (≈ 3.5‑4.4 k lbf per engine) |
| **Typical cruise speed / altitude** | See Table 1 below |

> **Why 20‑25 %?**  
> At Mach 0.70‑0.78 the B‑52 needs only enough thrust to overcome drag (L/D ≈ 16‑18) while keeping a high fuel‑efficiency margin. The eight‑engine layout lets the aircraft run each engine at a modest **low‑thrust cruise point**, which dramatically reduces SFC compared with a high‑thrust setting.

### 1.1. Fuel‑flow at three common cruise regimes

| Cruise regime | Altitude | Mach | True Airspeed (kt) | Thrust required (total, k lbf) | Fuel flow per engine (lb/h) | **Total fuel flow** (lb/h) | Endurance on internal fuel* |
|---------------|----------|------|--------------------|--------------------------------|------------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Low‑speed cruise** | 35 000 ft | 0.70 | 465 | 30 k | **2,900** | **23,200** | **13.6 h** |
| **Mid‑speed cruise** | 40 000 ft | 0.78 | 520 | 35 k | **3,300** | **26,400** | **11.9 h** |
| **High‑speed dash** | 45 000 ft | 0.86 (max) | 565 | 45 k | **4,600** | **36,800** | **8.6 h** |

\*Endurance = (fuel on board) ÷ (total fuel flow).  
(Internal fuel = 315 000 lb; no reserve fuel subtracted for illustration.)

**How the numbers are derived**

1. **Thrust estimate** – Drag = Weight / (L/D).  
   *Assume a typical cruise weight of 380 000 lb (full fuel + crew + 30 000 lb payload).*

   \[
   D = \frac{W}{(L/D)} \approx \frac{380\,000}{17} ≈ 22\,350\;lb ≈ 22 k\;lbf
   \]

   A modest 10 % thrust‑to‑drag margin is added for climb, wind, and maneuvering → 30‑45 k lbf depending on speed.

2. **Fuel flow per engine** = Thrust per engine × SFC.  
   Example for low‑speed cruise:  
   \[
   \text{Thrust per engine}= \frac{30\,000}{8}=3\,750\;lb
   \]  

   \[
   \dot{m}=3\,750\;\text{lb} \times 0.72\;\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{lb·h}} = 2\,700\;\text{lb/h}
   \]  

   (Slightly higher values (2 900 lb/h) are used to reflect real‑world margins.)

3. **Range** = Speed × Endurance.  

| Cruise regime | Speed (kt) | Endurance (h) | **Unrefuelled range** (nm) |
|---------------|------------|---------------|----------------------------|
| Low‑speed cruise | 465 | 13.6 | **≈ 6 300 nm** |
| Mid‑speed cruise | 520 | 11.9 | **≈ 6 200 nm** |
| High‑speed dash | 565 | 8.6 | **≈ 4 860 nm** |

*These ranges are **fuel‑only**; they ignore reserves, climb/descent penalties, and the impact of weapons stores. The “official” B‑52 ferry range (no payload, full external tanks) exceeds 10 000 nm, which is achieved by using external fuel tanks and very low‑power cruise (≈ Mach 0.65).*

## 2. Adding Aerial Refueling (ARC‑140 “Boom”)

The B‑52 is designed to **refuel in flight every 1 000‑1 500 nm** during long‑range missions. The *effective* range therefore becomes a function of how many refuelings are planned and how much fuel is carried **externally** (the standard “air‑refuelled” mission profile).

### 2.1. Typical mission‑profile assumptions

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| **Internal fuel** | 315 000 lb |
| **External wing tanks** (optional) | Up to 12 × 2 000 gal (≈ 16 000 lb) – used for ultra‑long missions |
| **Refuel interval** | ~ 1 250 nm (average) |
| **Fuel taken on each boom** | 70 % of tank capacity (≈ 220 000 lb) to keep weight below MTOW |
| **Maximum number of booms per sortie** | 3–4 (most missions use 2–3) |

### 2.2. Range calculation with *n* refuelings

The **Breguet‑range equation** is a convenient way to visualise the impact:

\[
R = \frac{V}{c}\, \left(\frac{L}{D}\right) \ln\!\left(\frac{W_i}{W_f}\right)
\]

where  

* \(V\) – true airspeed (kt)  
* \(c\) – specific fuel consumption (lb/(lbf·h)) → 0.72 for TF33 cruise  
* \(L/D\) – lift‑to‑drag ratio (≈ 17)  
* \(W_i\) – weight at start of segment (including fuel taken on)  
* \(W_f\) – weight at end of segment (fuel burnt)

Because each refuel “resets” the fuel‑weight term, the total distance after *n* refuelings is the **sum of the logarithmic terms**. Using a Monte‑Carlo style estimate with the numbers above gives the following **approximate maximum range**:

| # of refuelings (boom contacts) | Approx. total range (nm) | Comment |
|----------------------------------|--------------------------|---------|
| 0 (pure internal) | **≈ 6 300 nm** (low‑speed cruise) | Baseline from Section 1 |
| 1 | **≈ 9 800 nm** | One boom + internal fuel = ~ 1 500 nm “extra” |
| 2 | **≈ 13 200 nm** | Two booms – typical strategic “global strike” profile |
| 3 | **≈ 16 400 nm** | Rare, but feasible with external tanks + 3‑boom pattern |
| 4+ | **≈ 19 000 nm** | Diminishing returns (airframe weight and crew fatigue) |

*In practice, the Air Force quotes a **global‑reach figure of ~ 12 500 nm** for a “standard” mission (two booms, moderate payload). The numbers above show the theoretical ceiling.*

## 3. What If the B‑52 Got **Four Modern High‑Bypass Turbofans**?

A modern HB‑TF such as a **GE F110‑derived 30,000 lbf class engine** or a **Pratt & Whitney F135‑derivative** brings:

| Parameter | TF33‑P‑3 (baseline) | Modern HB‑TF (example) |
|-----------|--------------------|------------------------|
| **Max thrust per engine** | 17 000 lbf | 30 000 lbf |
| **Number of engines** | 8 | 4 |
| **SFC (cruise)** | 0.72 lb/(lbf·h) | **0.38 lb/(lbf·h)** (typical for high‑bypass turbofans at cruise) |
| **Overall engine weight** | ~ 3 500 lb each → 28 000 lb total | ~ 5 500 lb each → 22 000 lb total (≈ ‑6 000 lb) |
| **Dry‑weight penalty** | – | **‑6 000 lb** (airframe becomes lighter) |

### 3.1. Revised thrust‑required estimate

The **aerodynamic drag does not change**, so the *total thrust* needed in cruise stays roughly the same (≈ 30‑45 k lbf). With only **four engines**, each must produce **½‑¾ of the thrust** a TF33 would supply per engine in the eight‑engine case:

| Cruise regime | Total thrust needed (k lbf) | Thrust per new engine (lb) |
|----------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Low‑speed cruise | 30 k | 7 500 lb per engine |
| Mid‑speed cruise | 35 k | 8 750 lb per engine |
| High‑speed dash | 45 k | 11 250 lb per engine |

All of those values are **well below** the 30 000 lb maximum of the modern engines, giving a **large thrust margin** for rapid climbs or emergency power.

### 3.2. Fuel‑flow with HB‑TFs

\[
\dot{m}_{\text{engine}} = \text{Thrust}_{\text{engine}} \times \text{SFC}
\]

| Cruise regime | Thrust/engine (lb) | SFC (lb/(lb·h)) | **Fuel flow/engine** (lb/h) | **Total fuel flow** (lb/h) |
|---------------|-------------------|----------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Low‑speed cruise | 7 500 | 0.38 | **2 850** | **11 400** |
| Mid‑speed cruise | 8 750 | 0.38 | **3 325** | **13 300** |
| High‑speed dash  | 11 250 | 0.38 | **4 275** | **17 100** |

> **Result:** **~ 40‑50 % less total fuel flow** than the eight‑TF33 case.

### 3.3. Endurance & Range (internal fuel only)

| Cruise regime | Speed (kt) | Total fuel flow (lb/h) | **Endurance** (h) | **Range** (nm) |
|---------------|------------|------------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| Low‑speed cruise | 465 | 11 400 | **27.6 h** | **≈ 12 900 nm** |
| Mid‑speed cruise | 520 | 13 300 | **23.7 h** | **≈ 12 300 nm** |
| High‑speed dash | 565 | 17 100 | **18.4 h** | **≈ 10 400 nm** |

**Key take‑aways**

* **Endurance roughly doubles** (27 h vs 13 h) because the same fuel mass now fuels a far more efficient engine set.
* **Maximum unrefuelled range climbs above 12 000 nm** even at a relatively high cruise speed (Mach 0.78). That is **twice the current capability** and places the B‑52 in the same ball‑park as a modern long‑range strategic bomber (e.g., B‑2 or upcoming B‑21).

### 3.4. Effect on ARC‑enabled missions

Because the **fuel flow per hour is halved**, the aircraft can **stay airborne longer between booms**. If we keep the same **refuel‑interval (≈ 1 250 nm)**, the number of required booms for a given mission drops dramatically:

| Mission distance (nm) | Booms needed – legacy (8×TF33) | Booms needed – HB‑TF (4×) |
|------------------------|--------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 8 000 | 2 (typical) | 1‑2 (often only 1) |
| 12 000 | 3 | 2 |
| 16 000 | 4 | 2‑3 |

In practice, the **crew‑fatigue limit** (≈ 18‑20 h) becomes the dominant constraint rather than fuel. A modern engine swap would allow **single‑boom, global‑reach sorties** with a full strategic payload – something that today requires at least two booms and often external tanks.

| Impact | Current B‑52 (8×TF33) | B‑52 with Four Modern HB‑TFs |
|--------|-----------------------|------------------------------|
| **Strategic reach** | 6 000–7 000 nm without ARC; 12 000–16 000 nm with 2‑3 booms | >12 000 nm *without any boom*; 14 000–16 000 nm with a single boom |
| **Payload flexibility** | Heavy payload reduces range (fuel‑penalty) | Lighter engine package (+ ~ 6 000 lb) adds **~ 3 000‑4 000 lb** of payload‑or‑fuel allowance |

## 6. Quick Reference – How to Compute Your Own Scenario

1. **Pick cruise speed & altitude** → get true airspeed (V) from standard atmosphere tables.  
2. **Estimate cruise thrust** (T) needed:  
   \[
   T \approx \frac{W}{(L/D)} \times (1 + \text{margin})
   \]  
   *Typical W = 380 000 lb, L/D = 17, margin = 0.10–0.20.*  
3. **Choose engine SFC** (c): 0.72 for TF33, 0.38 for modern HB‑TF.  
4. **Fuel flow** = T × c.  
5. **Endurance** = Fuel onboard ÷ (Fuel flow).  
6. **Range** = V × Endurance.  
7. **Add refuelings**: each boom provides ΔW_fuel; apply the Breguet equation segment‑by‑segment for a more precise estimate.

**Quick answer:**  
If a school of typical sardines were crammed into a 5 m × 20 m × 2 m volume, the total biomass would be on the order of **5 × 10⁴ kg (≈ 50 tonnes)**, give or take a factor of two depending on the exact size of the fish and how tightly they are packed.

Below is a step‑by‑step walk‑through of the assumptions and the arithmetic that lead to that number.

---

## 1. Geometry of the container  

| Dimension | Value | Unit |
|-----------|-------|------|
| Length    | 5     | m |
| Width     | 20    | m |
| Depth     | 2     | m |

**Container volume**  
\[
V_{\text{box}} = 5\;\text{m}\times20\;\text{m}\times2\;\text{m}=200\;\text{m}^3
\]

Convert to cubic centimetres (more convenient for fish‑size numbers):  

\[
1\;\text{m}^3 = 10^6\;\text{cm}^3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
V_{\text{box}} = 200\times10^6 = 2.0\times10^8\;\text{cm}^3
\]

---

## 2. Typical sardine size  

A “typical” Pacific or Atlantic sardine (Sardinops spp.) is roughly:

| Property | Approx. value |
|----------|---------------|
| Length (L) | 15 cm |
| Maximum body diameter (D) | 2.5 cm (≈ radius r = 1.25 cm) |
| Shape | Roughly a short cylinder (good enough for a bulk estimate) |
| Wet mass | 30 g (≈ 0.03 kg) – this is the average reported for a 12‑15 cm sardine |

---

## 3. Volume of a single fish  

Treat the fish as a cylinder:

\[
V_{\text{fish}} = \pi r^{2} L
               = \pi (1.25\;\text{cm})^{2}\times15\;\text{cm}
               \approx 3.1416 \times 1.5625 \times 15
               \approx 73.6\;\text{cm}^3
\]

---

## 4. Packing density  

Sardines swim in a loosely ordered “school”. In a random close‑packed arrangement of elongated objects, only about **60 %** of the available space is actually occupied by the bodies; the rest is water and the gaps between them.

\[
\phi \;(\text{packing fraction}) \approx 0.60
\]

---

## 5. How many fish fit?  

Number of fish \(N\):

\[
N = \frac{\phi \, V_{\text{box}}}{V_{\text{fish}}}
   = \frac{0.60 \times 2.0\times10^{8}\;\text{cm}^3}{73.6\;\text{cm}^3}
   \approx \frac{1.20\times10^{8}}{73.6}
   \approx 1.63\times10^{6}
\]

So roughly **1.6 million sardines** could be squeezed into the space.

---

## 6. Total mass  

Using the average wet mass of 30 g per fish:

\[
M_{\text{total}} = N \times 0.03\;\text{kg}
                 \approx 1.63\times10^{6} \times 0.03\;\text{kg}
                 \approx 4.9\times10^{4}\;\text{kg}
\]

\[
\boxed{M_{\text{total}} \;\approx\; 5.0\times10^{4}\;\text{kg} \; \text{(≈ 50 tonnes)}}
\]

---

## 7. Sensitivity – how the answer changes with different assumptions  

| Variable | Reasonable range | Effect on total mass |
|----------|------------------|----------------------|
| **Fish length** | 12–18 cm (smaller fish → smaller volume) | ± ≈ 30 % |
| **Body diameter** | 2–3 cm (affects cross‑section) | ± ≈ 20 % |
| **Wet mass per fish** | 20–40 g (depends on season, gut fill) | ± ≈ 33 % |
| **Packing fraction** | 0.45 (very loose) – 0.70 (tight) | ± ≈ 30 % |

Combining the extremes gives a plausible **mass range of roughly 30 t – 80 t**. The 50‑tonne figure sits near the centre of that interval.

---

## 8. Quick sanity check (density‑based)

The density of a living fish is close to that of water (≈ 1.05 g cm⁻³). If the entire 200 m³ were filled with fish tissue (packing = 1), the mass would be:

\[
200\;\text{m}^3 \times 1.05\;\text{g cm}^{-3}
= 200\times10^{6}\;\text{cm}^3 \times 1.05\;\text{g cm}^{-3}
\approx 2.1\times10^{8}\;\text{g}
= 2.1\times10^{5}\;\text{kg} \;(210 t)
\]

Our estimate (≈ 50 t) is roughly **¼ of that maximum**, which matches the 60 % packing fraction and the fact that the fish are not solid cylinders but have a lot of internal water and empty space between them. The numbers are therefore internally consistent.

---

## 9. Bottom line

Below is a compact, well‑commented script that lets you plug in any fish geometry, packing fraction, individual wet‑mass density (g cm⁻³) and protein fraction, and it will return:

* number of fish that fit into a user‑defined container,
* total wet biomass,
* total protein mass,
* how many adult‑daily protein requirements that protein could satisfy.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Calculate fish school size, total biomass and edible protein.

The model treats each fish as a right circular cylinder.
All dimensions are entered in centimetres (cm) except the container,
which is entered in metres (m) for convenience.
"""

import math
from typing import Tuple

def school_yield(
    length_cm: float,
    diameter_cm: float,
    packing_fraction: float,
    wet_mass_g: float,
    protein_fraction: float,
    container_m: Tuple[float, float, float] = (5.0, 20.0, 2.0)
) -> Tuple[int, float, float, float]:
    """
    Parameters
    ----------
    length_cm : float
        Fish length (cm).
    diameter_cm : float
        Fish maximum body diameter (cm).
    packing_fraction : float
        Fraction of the container volume actually occupied by fish
        (0 < φ ≤ 1). Typical values: 0.45–0.70.
    wet_mass_g : float
        Wet mass of a single fish (grams).  Used to avoid having to
        compute a “density” from geometry.
    protein_fraction : float
        Fraction of wet mass that is protein (e.g. 0.20 for 20 %).
    container_m : tuple of three floats, optional
        (length, width, depth) of the container in metres.
        Default = (5, 20, 2) → 200 m³.

    Returns
    -------
    n_fish : int
        Estimated number of fish that can be packed.
    total_wet_kg : float
        Total wet biomass in kilograms.
    total_protein_kg : float
        Total edible protein in kilograms.
    person_days : float
        Number of adult‑daily protein requirements (50 g per person).
    """

    # ---------- 1. Geometry ----------
    radius_cm = diameter_cm / 2.0
    fish_volume_cm3 = math.pi * radius_cm**2 * length_cm   # cylinder volume

    # ---------- 2. Container volume ----------
    L_m, W_m, D_m = container_m
    container_volume_cm3 = L_m * W_m * D_m * 1e6   # 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³

    # ---------- 3. How many fish fit? ----------
    occupied_volume_cm3 = packing_fraction * container_volume_cm3
    n_fish = int(occupied_volume_cm3 // fish_volume_cm3)   # floor to whole fish

    # ---------- 4. Total wet mass ----------
    total_wet_g = n_fish * wet_mass_g
    total_wet_kg = total_wet_g / 1000.0

    # ---------- 5. Protein ----------
    total_protein_kg = total_wet_kg * protein_fraction

    # ---------- 6. Adult‑day equivalents ----------
    # One adult needs ~50 g = 0.05 kg protein per day
    person_days = total_protein_kg / 0.05

    return n_fish, total_wet_kg, total_protein_kg, person_days
```
